The answer involves several layers of Georgia law — from damage caps and filing deadlines to procedural requirements that do not apply to other types of personal injury cases. For background on how medical negligence law works, the Cornell Law Institute's medical malpractice overview is a helpful starting point.

If you or a loved one was harmed by a doctor, surgeon, hospital, or other healthcare provider in Georgia, you are probably asking: is there a limit on what I can recover in a medical malpractice claim? The answer involves several layers of Georgia law — from damage caps and filing deadlines to procedural requirements that do not apply to other types of personal injury cases. For background on how medical negligence law works, the malpractice overview from Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute is a helpful starting point.

Georgia layers a two-year limitation, a five-year repose, an expert-affidavit filing rule and a gross-negligence standard for emergency care on top of ordinary negligence law. Understanding these limits before you file is essential — because failing to meet even one procedural requirement can result in your case being dismissed before it ever reaches a jury.

before:
Georgia no longer caps non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases. In 2005, the Georgia legislature passed a law (O.C.G.A. § 51-13-1) capping non-economic damages at $350,000 per provider and $1.05 million total. However, the Georgia Supreme Court struck down that cap as unconstitutional in Atlanta Oculoplastic Surgery, P.C. v. Nestlehutt (2010), ruling that it violated the right to a jury trial under the Georgia Constitution.

This means that today, there is no statutory cap on compensatory damages — including pain and suffering — in Georgia medical malpractice cases. A jury can award whatever amount it determines is fair and supported by the evidence.

However, Georgia does cap punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1). Exceptions exist when the defendant acted with specific intent to cause harm or was under the influence of drugs or alcohol, in which case punitive damages are uncapped.
after:
Georgia no longer caps non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases. In 2005, the Georgia legislature passed a law (O.C.G.A. § 51-13-1) capping non-economic damages at $350,000 against health care providers (no matter how many were sued), $350,000 per medical facility, and $1.05 million in total. However, the Georgia Supreme Court struck down those caps as unconstitutional in Atlanta Oculoplastic Surgery, P.C. v. Nestlehutt, 286 Ga. 731 (decided March 22, 2010), ruling that they violated the right to a jury trial under the Georgia Constitution. The statute is still printed in the Code but is void.

This means that today, there is no statutory cap on compensatory damages — including pain and suffering — in Georgia medical malpractice cases. A jury can award whatever amount it determines is fair and supported by the evidence. Under the 2025 tort-reform act (SB 68), lawyers may argue a dollar figure for pain and suffering only in closing and only if tied to the evidence (O.C.G.A. § 9-10-184), and medical bills are measured by the reasonable value of necessary care (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-1.1).

However, Georgia does cap punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1). The cap does not apply when the defendant acted with specific intent to cause harm or was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs, or in product liability cases.

Georgia imposes a two-year statute of limitations for medical malpractice claims under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71. The clock generally starts on the date the negligent act or omission occurred — not the date you discovered the injury.

This is a critical distinction. If a surgeon left a sponge inside you during an operation, the two-year clock starts on the date of the surgery — even if you did not discover the sponge until months or years later. Georgia's discovery rule (discussed below) provides a limited exception, but the outer time boundary is absolute.

before:
Even with the discovery rule, Georgia imposes an absolute five-year statute of repose under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71(b). This means that no medical malpractice lawsuit can be filed more than five years after the date the negligent act occurred — regardless of when the injury was discovered.

The only exception is for foreign objects left in the body (such as surgical sponges, instruments, or broken device components). In those cases, O.C.G.A. § 9-3-72 allows the patient to file within one year of discovering the foreign object, even if more than five years have passed since the surgery.

The main exception is for foreign objects left in the body (such as surgical sponges or instruments; fixation devices and prosthetics do not count). In those cases, O.C.G.A. § 9-3-72 allows the patient to file within one year of discovering the foreign object, even if more than five years have passed since the surgery. A child under five at the time of the malpractice has until the tenth birthday (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-73).

The Discovery Rule: When You Did Not Know Right Away

Georgia's discovery rule accounts for medical injuries that surface only later. Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71(b), the two-year statute of limitations begins running on the date the patient knew or should have known that they were injured by medical negligence — rather than the date the negligence occurred.

Common situations where the discovery rule applies:

  • Misdiagnosis or failure to diagnose — a doctor missed cancer that was visible on imaging, but the patient did not learn of the error until symptoms worsened months later
  • Medication errors — a pharmacy dispensed the wrong medication, and the adverse effects developed gradually
  • Surgical complications — internal damage from a procedure that did not produce symptoms until well after the surgery

However, the discovery rule does not eliminate the five-year statute of repose. Even if you did not discover the injury until year four, you still only have until year five to file suit.
after:
When the Clock Starts Later: Misdiagnosis and Fraud

Georgia does not start the clock when you learn of the malpractice. But when a misdiagnosed condition later produces a new injury after a symptom-free period, the two years run from when that new injury's symptoms first appear (Amu v. Barnes). Fraud by the provider pauses the limitation, but not the repose, until the fraud is discovered (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-96).

Common situations where the injury comes later than the mistake:

  • Misdiagnosis or failure to diagnose — a doctor missed cancer that was visible on imaging, and it later became a new, worse injury; the clock starts when those new symptoms appear
  • Medication errors — a pharmacy dispensed the wrong medication, and the adverse effects surfaced later; the clock starts at the first symptoms
  • Surgical complications — internal damage from a procedure; the clock starts at the first symptoms, not a later diagnosis

None of this moves the five-year statute of repose. Even if the new injury surfaced in year four, you still only have until year five to file suit.

One of the most significant procedural hurdles in Georgia medical malpractice cases is the expert affidavit requirement under O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1. When you file a medical malpractice lawsuit, you must simultaneously file an affidavit from a qualified medical expert who has reviewed the case and concluded that:

  1. The healthcare provider deviated from the applicable standard of care
  2. That deviation was the proximate cause of the patient's injury

The expert must be a licensed healthcare professional who is competent to testify about the standard of care in the defendant's specialty. Filing a lawsuit without this affidavit — or with an affidavit from an unqualified expert — will result in dismissal.
after:
One of the most significant procedural hurdles in Georgia medical malpractice cases is the expert affidavit requirement under O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1. When you file a medical malpractice lawsuit, you must simultaneously file an affidavit from a qualified medical expert who has reviewed the case. The affidavit must:

  1. Identify at least one specific negligent act or omission by the provider
  2. Set out the factual basis for that claim

The expert must be a licensed healthcare professional who is competent to testify about the standard of care in the defendant's specialty. Filing without the affidavit means dismissal. A defective affidavit — including one from an unqualified expert — can be cured only by amending within 30 days of the defendant's motion (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1(e)).

before: If medical malpractice caused a patient's death, Georgia law allows the surviving spouse or next of kin to file a wrongful death claim. The two-year statute of limitations runs from the date of death (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71(a)).
after: If medical malpractice caused a patient's death, Georgia law allows the surviving spouse — or, if there is none, the children (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-2) — to file a wrongful death claim for the full value of the decedent's life (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-1). The two-year statute of limitations runs from the date of death (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71(a)), but the five-year statute of repose still runs from the negligent act.
